title: Digging in the desert
hookLine: a caravan out of water; a boy hammers through the rock and finds it (Jataka 2)

cards: The sand is too hot to cross by day, so the caravan travels at night, steered by a guide who reads the stars. Late in the journey, the guide falls asleep. The oxen wander, turn, and walk all night in a circle.
At dawn the merchants see their own campsite from yesterday. Their water and firewood are gone. That's where the second tale of the Jataka begins: lost, dry, and back at the start.

teach.h: THEY LIE DOWN AND GIVE UP.
teach.b: First, the despair. The caravan people lie down under their carts and give up. The leader, the bodhisatta, thinks: if I give up too, everyone dies.
So while it's still cool, he walks the camp, looking.
Second, the grass. He finds a clump of kusa grass growing in the sand. Grass means water somewhere below, he reasons.
He has the men dig, deep into the ground, until the spades hit rock. Nothing. The men drop their tools.
The bodhisatta climbs down into the pit and lays his ear against the stone. Underneath, faintly, he hears water running. He turns to a serving boy.
If you give up, he tells him, we're all lost. Go down with the hammer, and strike the rock. Fourth, the boy.
The boy goes down when the grown men have quit.
He swings the hammer, again and again, and the rock splits. Water rises up the shaft, the tale says, as tall as a palm tree. Everyone drinks, cooks, rests, and travels on.
The frame story is about a monk who'd given up on his practice, and the Buddha tells him this tale to remind him that in a past life he was the boy with the hammer. Look at who saves the caravan.
Not the leader, not the men with the spades.
A serving boy, doing one more swing.

how: Buddhist teachers tell this tale to encourage effort, viriya, one of the perfections, especially to people who have grown discouraged in their practice.

o: anger that drives you to fight
luck that turns up when needed

games.q: digging in the desert: tap the pairs.
p: fell asleep, and the oxen turned back
laid his ear against the rock
swung the hammer until it split

s: the caravan ran dry because it was attacked
the guide fell asleep and the oxen walked them back to their old campsite.
the leader heard water through the rock
he put his ear to the stone and heard it running underneath.
the strongest digger broke through the rock
the men quit; a serving boy kept swinging.

games.q: you're the serving boy. the men have dug deep and hit rock and given up. the leader hands you the hammer. what do you do?
o: refuse. if the men couldn't, you can't.
go down and swing until the rock breaks.
dig a new pit somewhere else.
games.why: the boy goes down and strikes the rock until it splits, and water rises up the shaft for the whole caravan.

practice: Picture one thing you stopped working on because it hit rock: a project, a conversation, a habit. Don't promise to finish it; just listen, the way the bodhisatta listened through the stone, for anything running underneath.
If something is there, name one small swing you could take; if not, that's information too, so rest.

wordCard.voice: Viriya. Effort, energy: what a boy showed, swinging a hammer until the water came, after a lost caravan's pit hit rock. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali viriya: effort, energy. it's one of the ten perfections, and this tale is told for it.

carryVoice: Your line: dig once more. Sometimes the water is just one more swing away. Rest well.
